Thailand has two mobile networks: AIS and True (which merged with dtac in 2023 and shares its network). Tourist SIMs with unlimited data cost about 449–499 THB for 8 days, 699 THB for 15 days and 1,199 THB for 30 days; you need your passport to register, and a tourist SIM is valid for a maximum of 60 days. Travel eSIMs run on the same two networks, and in Opensignal's August 2026 report AIS won the awards for coverage and consistent quality, which matters on an island with hills and boat trips.

Last checked: November 2026. Prices include VAT and are as listed by the operators and recent reviews in October 2026. Operators change packages often; check the price on the pack before you pay.

AIS or True?

AISTrue (and dtac)
NetworkThailand's largest operatorMerged True and dtac network (2023); both brands still sell SIMs
Opensignal, August 2026Best coverage, 5G coverage and consistent qualitydtac: fastest average downloads (about 41 Mbps); True: wide 5G availability
Best forIslands, hills, boat days, national parksFast data in Chaweng, Lamai and Bophut
Tourist SIM range1 day to 60 days8, 15 or 30 days, plus a 10-day data-only SIM

On Samui's main coast both networks are fast, with 4G and 5G in the towns. The difference shows in the interior hills, on the quieter south and west coasts and out at sea, where AIS generally holds a signal for longer. If you can, ask your hotel which network works best in your room: thick walls and hillside villas can make a big difference.

True's own site lists the 8-day Infinite SIM at 449 THB, while some True product pages show 499 THB. AIS also sells cheaper packs with a fixed data allowance instead of unlimited data. "Unlimited" plans are subject to fair-use rules, but in practice they handle video calls, maps and streaming for a holiday without trouble.

Registration rules

  • Passport required: every SIM must be registered in person with your passport. The shop scans it and takes your photo, which takes 5–15 minutes.
  • Limit: foreigners can hold up to 3 SIMs per operator, under rules updated by the telecoms regulator in May 2026.
  • 60-day maximum: a tourist SIM is valid for 60 days at most and can't be extended by topping up. To keep the number longer, re-verify your identity with your passport at an operator shop, or call 1242 (True) or 1678 (dtac).
  • Don't lend your SIM: numbers registered to you can be traced if used in scams.

AIS and True also sell their own tourist eSIMs, which you can buy online and register with your passport. A Thai number helps with Grab, WhatsApp bookings, deliveries and banks, so long-stayers usually want one. Check your phone is unlocked and supports eSIM before you buy one.

Roaming from home

Daily roaming passes from home operators typically cost the equivalent of about 6–12 US dollars or pounds a day, so a 2-week holiday can cost more than 100 in roaming alone. A Thai SIM or eSIM for 30 days costs about 1,199 THB. If you need your home number for bank security codes, keep it active in your phone's second SIM or eSIM slot with data roaming switched off; texts still arrive.

Calling and messaging in Thailand

Most Thais use LINE for messages and calls, and many businesses on Samui, from scooter shops to restaurants, also answer on WhatsApp. Grab needs mobile data and works best with a Thai number for driver calls; see getting around Koh Samui. Emergency numbers (1669 ambulance, 191 police, 1155 Tourist Police) work from any Thai SIM, including data-only tourist SIMs, which can still call emergency numbers.

Where to buy on Koh Samui

  • Bangkok airports: if you connect through Suvarnabhumi, the AIS and True counters in the arrivals hall are open long hours and the staff set everything up for you.
  • Samui Airport: see our Samui Airport guide for arrivals facilities. Operator counters have operated in the arrivals area, but opening hours are limited; don't count on them for a late arrival. [check]
  • Operator shops: bring your passport to an AIS or True shop for registration and help with settings. AIS and True have shops in Central Samui (Chaweng) and in the big supermarkets on the ring road. [check]
  • Phone shops: small mobile shops in Chaweng, Lamai and Nathon sell SIMs and top-ups and can register you.
  • 7-Eleven: sells top-up credit for both networks, but not tourist SIMs.

Quick setup checklist

  1. Before you fly, check your phone is unlocked (ask your home operator) and supports eSIM if you want one.
  2. Note your home SIM's PIN and keep the SIM tray tool or a pin in your wallet.
  3. Download offline maps of Samui and your boarding passes in case you land without data.
  4. Buy your SIM with your passport, and test data, a call and a text before you leave the counter.
  5. Write down the expiry date of your package; tourist SIMs stop working at 60 days at the latest.
  6. Add the Thai number to your Grab, hotel and tour bookings so drivers and guides can reach you.

Coverage on the island and at sea

  • Coastal towns: strong 4G and 5G in Chaweng, Lamai, Bophut, Maenam, Choeng Mon and Nathon.
  • Hills and interior: signal drops on the steep roads to the waterfalls and viewpoints and in some valleys. Download offline maps before you ride.
  • South and west coasts: generally fine in villages; patchier on the hillside roads around Taling Ngam and the route 4170 connector.
  • At sea: you'll have signal for much of the way to Pig Island, Koh Tan and Koh Phangan. Coverage around the outer islands of Ang Thong National Marine Park is patchy, and you shouldn't rely on it. [check]

A day with little signal at Ang Thong is part of the charm: the park is closed from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December, so book the Ang Thong speedboat day tour (1,800 THB adult) for later dates. Pig Island runs all year on the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult). Keep your phone in a waterproof pouch on the boat.

Wi-Fi in hotels, cafés and coworking spaces

Almost every hotel, guesthouse, villa and café on Samui has free Wi-Fi. Quality varies a lot: a resort with fibre to every room can be excellent, while a hillside villa on a shared connection may struggle with video calls.

  • Ask before you book: request a speed test screenshot from the room, not the lobby.
  • Cafés: many cafés in Bophut, Chaweng and Lamai advertise fast Wi-Fi and welcome laptops outside peak meal times.
  • Coworking: Samui has dedicated coworking spaces aimed at remote workers. See our digital nomad guide.
  • Back-up: an unlimited tourist SIM makes a good hotspot when the Wi-Fi fails.
  • Security: avoid banking on open public Wi-Fi; use your mobile data or a VPN.

Home internet for long stays

If you rent a villa or condo for months, a home fibre line is worth it. Coverage depends on the street, especially in the hills, so ask the provider to check your exact address before signing a rental contract. The main providers on Samui are AIS Fibre (which now includes the former 3BB network), True Online and the state operator NT. [check]

  • You usually need your passport and a Thai phone number; some providers ask for a deposit or a minimum contract.
  • Installation typically takes a few days after you sign up.
  • Ask your landlord whether a line is already installed; transferring it is faster than a new connection.
  • Keep a mobile hotspot as a back-up for storm outages.

Long-stay villas with tested internet are on our Koh Samui villas page; see also our long-stay guide.

Power, plugs and outages

  • Voltage: 220 V, 50 Hz. Most phone and laptop chargers handle this; check hair dryers and other appliances from 110 V countries.
  • Plugs: most sockets take both two flat pins (US style) and two round pins (European style); Thailand's own standard three-pin socket is also common. UK and Australian plugs need an adapter.
  • Outages: short power cuts happen, especially during storms in the October–December monsoon. Hillside villas and the west coast are hit more often.
  • Protect your gear: use a surge protector for laptops, and keep a charged power bank for boat days and outages.
